name: ls
description: Lists directory contents, showing file and folder names with optional details such as permissions, size, and modification time.

flags.description: Use a long listing format showing permissions, owner, group, size, and modification time.
Show all entries, including hidden files whose names start with a dot.
With -l, print human-readable sizes (e.g. 4.0K, 12M) instead of raw bytes.
Sort by modification time, newest first.
Sort by file size, largest first.

examples.explanation: With no arguments, ls lists the contents of the current directory in alphabetical order.

examples.output:
-rw-r--r-- 1 user user  220 Jan 10 09:15 notes.txt
drwxr-xr-x 2 user user 4096 Jan 12 14:02 projects
examples.explanation: Long format: the first character is the file type (d = directory, - = regular file), followed by the permission bits, link count, owner, group, size, modification date, and name.

examples.output:
drwxrwxr-x 12 root syslog 4.0K Jan 12 08:00 .
drwxr-xr-x 14 root root  4.0K Jan  5 21:10 ..
-rw-rw-r--  1 root utmp   292K Jan 12 08:00 lastlog
examples.explanation: Combines long format, hidden files, and human-readable sizes to inspect a system log directory.

examples.output:
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 6.4K Jan 11 17:30 nginx.conf
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  917 Jan  2 11:04 sysctl.conf
examples.explanation: Lists only .conf files, newest first. Useful for finding recently changed configuration files.

about: ls is one of the most frequently used commands on any Linux system. It reads directory entries and, in long mode, calls stat() on each entry to display metadata. GNU ls supports many sorting and formatting options that can be combined freely.
On macOS/BSD, ls is a different implementation: the common options (-l, -a, -h) behave the same, but some GNU options such as --group-directories-first are unavailable.
useCases: Inspect what is in a directory before deleting or modifying files.
Check file sizes and timestamps with ls -lh.
Find recently modified files with ls -lt.
mistakes: Typing LS in uppercase — Linux commands are case-sensitive, so LS gives "command not found".
Assuming ls output is sorted by date by default; it is sorted alphabetically unless you pass -t or -S.
warnings: Piping ls output into other commands is fragile when filenames contain spaces or newlines. Prefer find -print0 with xargs -0 for scripting.
distroNotes: GNU ls (coreutils) is standard on Linux. BSD/macOS ls uses different flags for some features (e.g. -G for color instead of --color).
